== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern / Not applicable for panel attrition (secondary cross-sectional spatial census of districts and DAC places); however, missing administrative records introduce bias because irrigation districts with "no record" of surface water delivery were imputed as zero delivery rather than analyzed for missingness, and Kings County LAFCO lacked updated boundary files (relying on 2015 DWR boundaries).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern — no confounding variables were controlled for in either the historical-era irrigation district comparisons or the ID-DAC (n = 97) vs. GDC (n = 56) comparisons. Bivariate Wilcoxon tests do not adjust for substantial baseline differences such as population size (mean 9,899 in ID-DACs vs. 20,515 in GDCs, p = 0.0035), municipal incorporation, presence of domestic/municipal drinking-water utilities, aquifer hydrogeology, or spatial clustering across counties.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate concern — legal/institutional classifications (Wright Act of 1887, pre-1914 senior vs. post-1914 SWRCB appropriative water rights, SGMA, and LAFCO irrigation district boundaries) draw on official state/local registries (LAFCO, eWRIMS, USBR contracts, GSPs, AWMPs) verified with district managers, but surface water rights are modeled at 100% face allocation, "no record" deliveries are assumed zero, Kings County uses older 2015 DWR boundaries, and agricultural irrigation district boundaries are conflated with local drinking-water governance despite excluding domestic and municipal water agencies.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern — groundwater reliance is not measured from metered pumping but inferred as a simplified steady-state water-budget residual combining asynchronous periods (2001–2015, 2005–2019, or 2008–2019 average surface deliveries minus 2016 Land IQ/WAFR crop evapotranspiration demand), imputing "no record" deliveries as zero; additionally, census-tract CalEnviroScreen 4.0 percentiles are linked to DAC census places via spatial centroids, and GDCs are defined solely by falling outside agricultural irrigation districts without verifying municipal/domestic water system service.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-high concern — district groundwater reliance is an unvalidated modeled residual ignoring storage change, conveyance/recharge losses, and lateral groundwater flow, while community drinking-water and environmental outcomes rely on census-tract screening percentiles (2018 OEHHA CalEnviroScreen 4.0) joined to DAC place centroids rather than direct community water-system quality or household access measurements.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern — no pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is reported, formal statistical tests across the four historical formation eras are omitted, and the clustering algorithm, distance metric, and cluster-count selection criteria for the 5-group typology (Section 3.4, Fig 5) are not specified in the manuscript text, although underlying datasets and R scripts are publicly archived on Dryad and GitHub.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Low-to-moderate concern — the study covers the full census of agricultural irrigation districts and all 153 DWR-mapped 2018 DAC census places (97 ID-DACs and 56 GDCs) on the San Joaquin Valley floor across eight counties, avoiding survey non-response; however, excluding domestic, municipal, and water conservation agencies while classifying all DACs outside agricultural irrigation districts as "groundwater-dependent communities" creates structural frame misclassification regarding domestic water service.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are explicitly defined for both units of analysis: water agencies on the eight-county San Joaquin Valley floor that distribute agricultural irrigation water (explicitly excluding water conservation, domestic, and municipal water agencies), and all 2018 DWR-mapped disadvantaged community (DAC) census places on the valley floor classified into ID-DACs (n = 97) and GDCs (n = 56), although the exact total count of irrigation districts is only inferable across cluster summaries rather than stated in one sentence in Section 2.2.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 6–9, Sections 2.2 and 2.4; Figure 2; PDF Page 13, Section 3.3 and Table 1

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The geographic, hydrological, institutional, and historical setting of California's San Joaquin Valley floor is described in detail across four historical water-development eras (1887–2020), five regional irrigation-district cluster profiles, and socioeconomic/environmental profiles of the 97 ID-DACs and 56 GDCs.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4–8, Sections 1.2–1.4 and 2.2; PDF Pages 10–16, Sections 3.1–3.4, Table 1, and Figures 2–5

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Institutional exposures use official state/county sources (LAFCO boundaries for 7 counties, SWRCB eWRIMS water rights, USBR contracts, GSPs, AWMPs, and PPIC delivery records) cross-checked with district managers, but reliability and validity are weakened by using 2015 DWR boundaries for Kings County, combining mismatched delivery windows (2001–2015 vs. 2005–2019 and 2008–2019), assuming 100% of claimed water-right allocations, imputing "no record" deliveries as zero, joining DACs via census place centroids, and classifying DACs outside agricultural irrigation districts as groundwater-dependent (GDCs) despite having excluded municipal/domestic water agencies.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 7–9, Sections 2.2–2.4; PDF Page 12, Figure 4 caption; PDF Page 18, Acknowledgments

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Statutory water-right seniority (pre-1914 vs. post-1914 appropriative rights under the Water Commission Act of 1914), LAFCO/DWR jurisdictional boundaries, and state-designated Disadvantaged Community (DAC) census place definitions from the 2018 DWR DAC Mapping Tool follow objective, standardized California regulatory criteria.

Although the narrative notes regional crop patterns, historical land-value taxation, and mean population differences between ID-DACs (9,899) and GDCs (20,515), the authors do not identify or conceptualize confounding variables (e.g., city incorporation, domestic/municipal water utility coverage, population scale, local hydrogeology, or county-level regulatory differences) that could confound the cross-sectional relationship between irrigation district boundaries/seniority and community drinking-water or pollution burdens.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 9–10, Section 2.4; PDF Pages 13–14, Section 3.3 and Table 1

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: No analytical strategies to address confounding (such as multivariable regression, covariate adjustment, matching, stratification by incorporation/population size, or spatial error modeling) are stated or implemented in any part of the analysis.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 8–10, Sections 2.2–2.4; PDF Page 13, Section 3.3 and Table 1

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Outcomes suffer from key measurement and modeling limitations: (1) irrigation district groundwater reliance is not directly observed pumping, but an uncalibrated steady-state water-balance residual subtracting 2016 modeled crop evapotranspiration (Land IQ + WAFR) from 2001–2015 average surface deliveries (with "no record" imputed as zero and storage change/lateral groundwater flow omitted); and (2) community drinking-water and environmental burdens rely on census-tract screening percentiles (2018 CalEnviroScreen 4.0) spatially matched to DAC census place centroids rather than direct system-level water access/quality data.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 8–9, Sections 2.3–2.4; PDF Page 12, Figure 4 caption; PDF Page 13, Table 1

domain_ratings.justification: Statistical analysis relies on 10 unadjusted bivariate unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon tests (inaccurately described in Section 2.4 as "comparing the mean of the variables" while reporting means rather than medians/ranks in Table 1) with no adjustment for multiple testing, spatial autocorrelation, or major confounders; furthermore, the clustering method, distance metric, and cluster validation criteria for the 5-cluster typology (Fig 5) and formal statistical tests across formation eras (Fig 3B) are not reported in the manuscript text.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 7–10, Sections 2.1, 2.2, and 2.4; PDF Page 13, Table 1; PDF Pages 14–15, Section 3.4 and Figure 5

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This analytical cross-sectional geospatial study compiles state and county administrative datasets across California's San Joaquin Valley floor to examine how historical irrigation district formation eras and water-right seniority relate to modeled groundwater reliance and crop composition, and whether Disadvantaged Communities inside irrigation district boundaries (ID-DACs, n = 97) differ in environmental and drinking-water burdens from DACs outside irrigation districts (GDCs, n = 56). Strengths include comprehensive regional coverage across eight counties, transparent open data/code archiving (Dryad and GitHub), and grounding in official statutory and administrative registries (LAFCO, SWRCB eWRIMS, Land IQ, DWR DAC Mapping Tool, and OEHHA CalEnviroScreen 4.0). However, overall methodological risk of bias is rated High concern under the JBI Analytical Cross-Sectional Checklist due to three core limitations: (1) complete absence of confounding identification and adjustment in both district-era comparisons and bivariate ID-DAC vs. GDC Wilcoxon tests (despite GDCs having more than twice the mean population of ID-DACs and unmeasured differences in municipal incorporation and domestic water-utility service); (2) exposure and outcome measurement vulnerabilities, including imputing "no record" surface water deliveries as zero, modeling groundwater reliance indirectly from asynchronous periods (2001–2015 deliveries vs. 2016 crop evapotranspiration), joining census-tract CalEnviroScreen percentiles via DAC place centroids, and classifying non-irrigation-district DACs as groundwater-dependent after excluding municipal and domestic water agencies; and (3) unadjusted multiple bivariate testing alongside unspecified clustering methods in the main text.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional geospatial observational study (secondary spatial/administrative analysis comparing irrigation districts across historical formation eras/clusters and comparing disadvantaged communities inside vs. outside irrigation district boundaries at a single contemporary cross-section)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, data sources, inclusion/exclusion rules, water-budget modeling assumptions, spatial centroid joins, and statistical tests are reported in Section 2 (Materials and methods, PDF Pages 6–10), with empirical comparisons, Table 1, and cluster profiles in Section 3 (Results and discussion, PDF Pages 10–16) and data/agency verification notes on PDF Pages 1 and 18.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The empirical analysis compiles cross-sectional spatial and administrative indicators (2016 Land IQ crop composition/revenue, multi-year average surface water deliveries collapsed into a single cross-sectional district metric, and 2018 DWR/CalEnviroScreen 4.0 community indicators) to perform observational cross-sectional comparisons across irrigation district formation eras/clusters and between ID-DACs (n = 97) and GDCs (n = 56) using descriptive statistics and unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon tests. Because there is no longitudinal panel tracking of outcomes over time and no quasi-experimental intervention evaluation structure (such as DiD, RDD, IV, ITS, or matching), the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching appraisal tool rather than ROBINS-I or JBI Cohort.
